articles.title: Shark bites fisherman twice during kayaking encounter along California beach
articles.summary: A Malibu shark encounter sent a kayaker to the hospital after he reportedly reeled in a suspected mako shark while fishing off the California coast.
articles.body: A kayaker fishing off a Malibu beach was rushed to a local hospital Sunday morning after a shark encounter reportedly left him with two bite wounds. The incident occurred near Paradise Cove in Los Angeles County, according to KTLA. Witnesses told the outlet that the fisherman had reeled in what was believed to be a mako shark and was attempting to release it when the animal bit him, causing him to fall into the water. The shark then bit him a second time before swimming away, according to reports. The Los Angeles County Fire Department initially described the incident as a shark attack but later characterized it as a "fishing accident," ABC 7 reported. SWIMMER RUSHED TO HOSPITAL AFTER SUSPECTED SHARK ATTACK AT MARTHA’S VINEYARD A manager at the nearby Paradise Cove Beach Cafe said he saw the victim's injuries near his legs. "He was bitten in two places," the manager told KTLA. "I saw there were some teeth marks on his lower leg and above the knee." AUSTRALIAN SURFER RISKED HIS LIFE TO SAVE FELLOW SURFER WHO HAD BEEN ATTACKED BY A SHARK Video captured a lifeguard rushing toward the fisherman moments after the attack, while a small fishing boat floated nearby. A fisherman reportedly rushed to the victim’s aid, pulled him from the water onto his boat, and brought the fisherman back to shore, KTLA said. The victim reportedly called his girlfriend, a retired lifeguard, who helped him from the boat, assisted him onshore and called for emergency responders. Los Angeles County Fire Department crews responded to the scene and took the victim to a local hospital, the outlet said. Recalling the incident, the cafe manager reportedly said, "We’ve had a lot of crazy stuff happen here, but we’ve never had a shark attack like that." The beach remained open following the incident, ABC 7 reported. Chances of encountering a shark in Southern California are higher in October, when warmer coastal waters attract both prey and juvenile sharks. Female sharks often use shallow, warmer waters as nursery grounds, where young sharks can feed and grow with relative protection. articles.title: Australia once paid bounties to kill kangaroos and other marsupials; up to 27 million animals were destroyed
articles.summary: Australia once used government-funded bounties to encourage people to kill native marsupials, including kangaroos, wallabies and bandicoots.
articles.body: Australia once used government-funded bounties to encourage people to kill native marsupials, including kangaroos, wallabies and bandicoots. A 2026 study published in Nature found that the programme led to the destruction of up to 27 million animals between the late 19th century and 1930. The scheme was introduced when the Queensland Government sought to reduce competition between native marsupials and livestock for food. Researchers examining historical bounty programmes around the world found that the Queensland campaign was one of the largest examples they identified.How did Australia’s bounty programme begin in QueenslandThe Queensland Government introduced the Marsupial Destruction Act in 1877. According to the study by Julian D. Olden and colleagues, the legislation was designed to encourage the killing of marsupials that were considered competitors with livestock for available feed.The government used financial rewards to make killing the animals an attractive activity. The programme remained in place until 1930, meaning that payments continued for more than five decades.The researchers recorded the Queensland scheme as part of a global study of bounty programmes used to control species considered unwanted. Their research examined records covering about 800 years and found hundreds of examples from different parts of the world.The programme covered animals other than kangaroosThe animals targeted in Queensland included several familiar kangaroo and wallaby species. The study identifies red kangaroos, eastern grey kangaroos and western grey kangaroos among the species covered by the legislation.Other animals included the agile wallaby, black-striped wallaby, red-necked wallaby and common wallaroo. Smaller marsupials were also affected, including the northern brown bandicoot, long-nosed bandicoot, long-footed potoroo and long-nosed potoroo.This broad list shows that the bounty was not limited to large kangaroos. A range of native marsupials was included in the programme because they were considered relevant to the same livestock-related concern.What was the scale of the killingThe numbers recorded by the researchers show how large the programme became. The study estimates that as many as 27 million marsupials were destroyed during the period covered by the Queensland bounty scheme. The government also paid about £1.187 million in bounties. The figure represents the financial cost of the system recorded by the researchers and gives an indication of how extensively the programme was used.Bounty schemes were used across the worldThe Queensland case was not an isolated approach to wildlife management. The researchers identified at least 283 species that had been targeted through bounty programmes, with examples recorded across 60 countries.Three-quarters of the programmes focused on terrestrial species, while the remainder involved freshwater or marine species. Australia was among the countries with the greatest number of species subject to bounty programmes in the researchers review.Mammals made up more than one-third of the species recorded in the study. Birds were another major group, while fish, reptiles, insects, amphibians, molluscs, crustaceans and plants also appeared in the historical records.Why were native species targetedThe researchers found that bounty schemes were often connected to practical concerns about human activities. These included protecting livestock, crops, fisheries and infrastructure, as well as concerns about ecosystems and human health.In Queensland, the specific reason recorded in the study was competition for feed between marsupials and livestock. Native animals were therefore treated as a problem in an agricultural setting where available food was considered valuable to farmed animals.The global review found that native species were actually the main focus of these programmes. About 69.5% of the 449 species-country programmes involved native species, while 30.5% involved non-native species.The historical record also shows problemsThe study found that bounty programmes did not always work exactly as intended. Financial rewards can change how people behave because payments create a direct incentive to kill animals.The researchers identified historical cases involving fraudulent claims and other unintended consequences. Some programmes also resulted in animals being killed beyond the species that authorities had intended to target.These problems matter because removing animals from an ecosystem can produce effects that are difficult to predict. The study highlights the importance of considering how a bounty is designed, what it is intended to achieve and whether its results are properly assessed.What the Queensland case tells about wildlife controlThe Queensland programme ended in 1930. Across different countries and time periods, governments have repeatedly used financial incentives to encourage people to remove species regarded as harmful or unwanted. The study does not treat every bounty programme as identical. Instead, it shows that their outcomes depended on the species involved, the reason for targeting them and how the programmes were organised.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Masha’s husband was fighting on the front line. But she was the one killed by a Russian drone
articles.summary: It was not meant to be Masha. Her husband, Danylo Yivzhenko, is the soldier in the family. Masha was a civilian, back home in Kyiv, worrying about her husband on the front line.
articles.body: It was not meant to be Masha. Her husband, Danylo Yivzhenko, is the soldier in the family. As a combat medic with Ukraine’s Third Separate Assault Brigade, he made the decision to go to war, knowing the risk. Masha was a civilian, back home in Kyiv, worrying about her husband on the front line. But it was Masha, 29, who was killed by the Russians when a powerful drone struck her office building in the Ukrainian capital on September 25. It’s an injustice that Yivzhenko cannot comprehend. “I am a soldier and I am fighting against Russia. If a Russian military drone or a ballistic missile, or whatever else, kills me – that is fair. We kill Russians. Russians kill us. We are servicemen; we understand what we are doing,” he told CNN. “Killing a soldier is horrible, but it is normal. But Masha was a civilian. She did not assemble drones, she did not hold a weapon in her hands, she did not wear a military uniform. She was a civilian in a civilian city who was simply doing her civilian job that day.” Daily life as it was known in Kyiv stopped on August 27, when Russia began pounding the city with near non-stop aerial assaults. Since then, not a single day has passed without an air raid warning in the city. On average, there have been seven air raid alerts a day. Some days, there have been as many as 13. The Ukrainian military is increasingly unable to defend Kyiv from these assaults because of critical shortages of air defense weapons to bring down Russia’s missiles and its newest jet-powered drones. Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelensky, has been begging allies to help, and the Ukrainian military is racing to develop effective interceptors domestically – but neither has yet led to a meaningful shift. In just over a month – between August 27 and Oct 4 – at least 98 people have been killed and 435 injured in Kyiv and the wider Kyiv region, a number that is significantly higher than in previous months. Several high-profile buildings at the heart of the capital have been struck by Russian drones during this period, including the headquarters of the Security Service of Ukraine, the National Academy of Sciences, High Council of Justice and a TV and internet provider’s data center. Russia consistently claims it only strikes military targets, despite ample evidence of civilian sites being struck on a regular basis. Russia used to launch its aerial attacks overnight under the cover of darkness, to minimize Kyiv’s chances of intercepting them. This meant people were often exhausted after a sleepless night in a shelter, but their lives could go on relatively as normal during the day. But Russia’s newest jet-powered drones have made it possible for Moscow to terrorize Ukraine at any time of the day. And each time Russia fires at Kyiv, an air raid alarm is triggered and life in the capital stops. Many businesses and services, including some public transit operations, shut down, and everyone is meant to head to a shelter. The Ukrainian capital is split in half by the Dnipro river. The right bank is home to the majority of Kyiv’s business centers, offices and government institutions, whereas the left bank is mostly residential. The bridges connecting the two sides are crucial – some 600,000 vehicles cross them every day. And these vital links have become the most recent target for Russia. Kyiv’s Southern Bridge, which serves ground transportation as well as the city’s subway system, was hit five times within two days on Thursday and Friday. The city’s Northern Bridge was hit twice on Saturday and Sunday. The disruption has forced Kyiv authorities to start work on creating a new pontoon bridge. Schoolchildren suffer Russia’s shift toward this new strategy coincided with the start of a new school year in Ukraine – and children are among those hit hardest by the constant interruptions. According to Kyiv authorities, roughly half of the city’s 250,000 children are attending schools in person full time, while most of the rest alternate between remote and in-person learning. A handful of schools are operating fully online. Some schools have gone as far as moving all of their classes underground. Others spend precious learning time moving children to shelters. The enormous risks of bringing children into classrooms were made clear on Thursday, when a Russian drone struck one of Kyiv’s schools while more than 100 children were inside. The school’s headteacher, Olena Chorna, said an earlier air raid alert had only just ended when the sirens started blaring again. “We all hurried down to the shelter and stayed there … 104 children were in the shelter. We could hear things being destroyed; the school was filled with smoke, but in the shelter all the doors were closed and we couldn’t feel a thing.” No one was injured but extensive damage was caused to the building. But with alerts now much more common, many find it hard to keep following the official guidance. “I can’t stay in shelters all the time, because I have to keep living, keep studying,” university student Sophia Zaremba told CNN. Zaremba, who is 20, said the day-to-day reality of living under fire was catching up with her. She witnessed a Russian drone strike next to her university building the day before speaking to CNN. She knew an air raid alert was in place, but she had urgent errands to take care of, she explained. “It was unexpected. You get used to the fact that drones are flying around and that there are various places nearby where they might hit… but this was loud, and it caught us off guard,” she said. She told CNN that all she could think of in the moment was that another explosion might be imminent. “I just thought the alarm was still going off and, God forbid, the next strike might be nearby.” All her remaining sense of security has been shattered, she added. “I haven’t been able to get out of bed for half the day today because I just don’t have the mental strength to do anything.” Russia’s current weapon of choice against Kyiv is its new wave of jet-powered drones, known as the Geran-4 and Geran-5. These killer machines resemble tiny cruise missiles, flying at speeds of up to 600 kilometers per hour (310 miles per hour) and often carrying powerful warheads. They often travel too fast and too high for Kyiv’s mobile fire groups to shoot down, so ground-to-air missiles, fighter jets or interceptors must be deployed – all of which are in extremely limited supply in Ukraine. At the same time, these drones cost as little as one-tenth as much as a traditional cruise missile to produce than traditional cruise missiles, which means Russia can afford to launch dozens of them at the same time. According to Yurii Ihnat, spokesman for the Ukrainian Air Force, Russia launched 2,850 jet-powered drones in August and 3,177 in September. Masha Yivzhenko was killed when her office building in central Kyiv was hit by a Geran-5 drone on September 25. According to Serhii Beskrestnov, an adviser to Zelensky, another jet-powered drone was circling the site of the strike at high altitude, providing a radio signal for the device. Once the building was struck, the second drone flew off to attack a McDonald’s warehouse in the suburbs of Kyiv, Beskrestnov said. Yivzhenko told CNN that one of the things he loved most about Masha was the fact the two of them — both former journalists – always had something interesting to talk about. “She was my best friend and my whole life was built around the fact that we had each other,” he said. When Yivzhenko enlisted in 2024, after working as a volunteer medic since the beginning of the war, the couple got a dog, Jessie, so that Masha wouldn’t be completely alone. They took out a mortgage to buy an apartment and were planning their future, despite the war. “We bought Masha a car because we were planning to have children,” he said. Yivzhenko was in Kyiv for a few days last week. On the day of the attack, he drove Masha to her office to pick up her laptop so she could work from home. She popped in for a few minutes and he walked Jessie while waiting for her to come back. And then the drone struck. First responders at the scene told Yivzhenko that his wife had died on impact. Her body was found under the stairs on the first floor of the office building. “She didn’t burn, she didn’t bleed to death. She died instantly. The blast wave threw her down from the fifth floor,” he told CNN. “I identified her, and they let me go. I have buried my brothers-in-arms and I am mentally prepared for the fact that I will bury my parents when they get old. And all of that is normal. That is life. But by killing Masha, they killed me.”

articles.title: Russian lab worker dies of suspected plague in Siberia; US monitoring case
articles.summary: A Russian agency links the lab worker’s death to ‘pneumonia of unknown’ origin.
articles.body:
An employee of a Russian anti-plague institute in the remote Siberian region of Irkutsk has reportedly died of a suspected pneumonic plague infection, according to a United States official.

“We are aware of reports of a fatal case of suspected pneumonic plague in Irkutsk Oblast, Russia. We are monitoring the situation closely with the CDC [Centers for Disease Control and Prevention] and our other interagency partners,” a State Department official told Al Jazeera

“Many details have not been confirmed. We encourage Russian authorities to share accurate information quickly and openly,” the official said.

Alexei Tsydenov, the governor of the Buryatia region, said in a post on his Telegram channel on October 3 that a woman in the neighbouring Irkutsk region had “died, maybe of the plague”.

Russia’s official TASS news agency reported on Sunday that the country’s consumer watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, said in a statement that an employee of the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East had been diagnosed with “pneumonia of unknown aetiology”.

The watchdog also said it expanded testing of samples from the patient and found no microorganisms associated with her professional activities.

Pneumonic plague is caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, usually found in small mammals and their fleas. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), the plague is highly infectious and can be fatal if not treated early.

Local media named the woman who died as 28-year-old laboratory technician Darya Shipilova.

Media reports say that authorities in Siberia’s Irkutsk region have placed nearly 200 people under medical observation.

articles.title: FBI arrests ‘Chinese foreign agent’ for spying on Taiwan president’s son
articles.summary: A California woman allegedly sent photos and videos of President Lai’s son and his family to Chinese officials.
articles.body:
The FBI has arrested a “Chinese foreign agent” at Los Angeles International Airport accused of spying on the Taiwanese president’s son.

Wanying Zhang, also known as Heather, was arrested on Sunday before her planned departure to China, the first assistant US attorney for the Central District of California, Bill Essayli, said in a post on X.

Authorities charged Zhang, 34, of Irvine, California, with acting as an unregistered foreign agent.

Zhang surveilled Taiwanese President William Lai Ching-te’s son, the FBI said. The agency did not directly name Zhang’s alleged target, but later shared a news article identifying him as Lai Ting-yu.

The US Justice Department said Zhang travelled to Seattle in 2025 at the behest of Chinese officials. She sent photos, video and license plate information of the Taiwanese leader’s son and his family to China.

Essayli called Zhang a “Chinese foreign agent” and said she “used tradecraft to avoid detection”.

“She never notified the Attorney General she was acting for a foreign government, a federal offense,” he added.

Essayli said Zhang will appear in a Los Angeles federal court on Monday.

William Lai Ching-te and his Democratic Progressive Party say that Taiwan is already an independent country separate from China. Beijing views the island as Chinese territory.

Washington does not have ⁠formal diplomatic ties with Taiwan, but the US is bound by law to provide the island with the means to ‌defend itself.

Earlier this week, the US delivered two F-16V ⁠Block 70 fighter jets to Taiwan as the island seeks to build its defence capabilities to deter a feared attack by China .

In January, Chinese President Xi Jinping pledged to achieve the “reunification” of China and Taiwan, calling Beijing’s long-held goal “unstoppable”.

articles.title: Samoan leader apologizes for ‘Heil Hitler’ salute at 2007 family reunion
articles.summary: Samoa’s prime minister has apologized after an old video of him surfaced performing the Nazi salute while leading a chorus of “Heil Hitler” at a family reunion in 2007.
articles.body: Samoa’s prime minister has apologized after an old video of him surfaced performing the Nazi salute while leading a chorus of “Heil Hitler” at a family reunion in 2007. Prime Minister Laaulialemalietoa Leuatea Schmidt said his words were “not intended for the public” and apologized in a statement published by the government Monday. “Whatever the context or intention at that gathering twenty years ago, I recognise that those words and gesture were inappropriate and capable of causing offence and hurt and I apologise for using them,” said Laaulialemalietoa, who became PM of the Pacific Island nation last year. The antisemitic remarks were made during a “private family gathering” in Savai’i, the country’s largest island, in 2007, Laaulialemalietoa said, when he was serving as deputy speaker of Parliament. In the seven-second video clip, Laaulialemalietoa is seen leading about a dozen people in the Nazi-affiliated salute, saying “Raise your right hand, Heil Hitler,” while the group mimics his words and gesture, according to the Samoa Observer newspaper, which first reported on the video Sunday. Laaulialemalietoa banned the Samoa Observer from all government press conferences last year for what he’s called “unfair” reporting. Samoa is a tiny nation of about 221,000 people in the South Pacific, near Fiji. It sits to the west of American Samoa, the US territory in the eastern part of the Samoan island chain. Samoa was colonized by Germany in the early 20th century, and many Samoans have German heritage and surnames. New Zealand took what was then known as Western Samoa from the Germans in 1914 and retained control of Samoa until the country’s independence in 1962. In his statement Monday, Laaulialemalietoa said his behavior in the clip does not reflect his personal beliefs or the beliefs of the government or people of Samoa. “I reject Nazism, antisemitism, racism and all forms of political extremism,” he said, adding that he now considers “this matter addressed.”

articles.title: New security lanes to speed up checks at Leeds Bradford Airport
articles.summary: Leeds Bradford passengers will also be able to leave liquids under 100ml in their hand luggage.
articles.body:
New technology means passengers using Leeds Bradford Airport (LBA) will have shorter waits for security checks, airport bosses have said.

A new Central Search Zone is opening, with extra-long security lanes allowing almost double the number of people to be screened per hour.

Passengers are also now able to leave electronics and liquids under 100ml in their bags, rather than having to take them out to be scanned separately.

The airport's management says it forms part of their long-term vision to modernise its infrastructure, improve operational efficiency and deliver an airport experience that meets the expectations of a growing region.

The new facility features dynamic virtual queue management, which means that LBA's team can actively manage passenger flow and reduce waiting times during busy periods.

The area also includes six eGates for boarding card scanning, helping passengers move efficiently into the security search area.

Individual lanes will be capable of processing up to 600 passengers per hour, compared with approximately 350 previously.

By the end of the year, a further two lanes will come into operation, doubling the airport's current security screening capacity.

Dedicated routes have been introduced for passengers needing special assistance, and Fast Track customers.

Vincent Hodder, CEO at LBA, described it as a "landmark moment".

"This is a truly transformational investment that will significantly enhance the passenger experience," he said.

"Not only are we increasing capacity, but we're introducing some of the most advanced security processing technology available at any UK regional airport.

"By doubling our current security capacity, we're creating a more efficient, more comfortable journey for our customers.

"Passengers will spend less time queuing and more time enjoying our terminal facilities before departure."

articles.title: Norfolk housing levy idea is flawed, say environmental groups
articles.summary: The government wants developers to fund waterways projects in Norfolk.
articles.body:
Environmental groups have criticised a pilot scheme that aims to make housing developers pay a new nature levy.

The government wants parts of Norfolk to be the first areas subject to its Environmental Delivery Plan (EDP).

In order to unlock space for thousands of homes, developers would pay money that could create new wetlands, fund deer culls and restore rivers.

But ecology experts fear that it would fail to tackle the sources of pollution, leaving vulnerable chalk streams still at risk.

Sally Haines, chief executive of the Chartered Institute of Ecology and Environmental Management, said: "While [actions outlined in the plan] would improve ecological habitats in the area, they won't necessarily address the pollution that will be going into the water.

"Unless you do that, you are not going to get good nature recovery."

The EDP, which would apply to much of central Norfolk and parts of The Broads, would pool cash from housebuilders.

It would be spent on measures to help offset pollution from new homes.

Norfolk's rare chalk streams, often described as England's rainforests, are particularly vulnerable.

Environment Secretary Angela Eagle calls it a "win-win" for development and nature, claiming it would unlock space for 15,780 homes that are currently stalled because of rules protecting rivers.

With developers paying £2,675 per house, it is hoped the levy will raise about £42m.

The scheme is designed to replace the more complicated nutrient neutrality rules that are in place, which were blamed for blocking the regeneration plan for the former Colman's Mustard Factory at Carrow Works in Norwich.

A government spokesperson said the introduction of a single levy would make life easier for developers.

Natural England is leading on the project and chief executive Marian Spain said: "Instead of tackling pollution piecemeal, site by site, we can now deliver conservation measures that make a real difference for rivers, wetlands and wildlife across Norfolk."

However, Haines said it was a "fallacy" to blame environmental concerns as the main stumbling block when building houses - pointing instead to a myriad of issues such as the availability of materials and labour, and land prices.

Under the proposals, restoration projects would be put together for the River Wensum , the Bure broads and marshes, and the River Yare catchment area.

One eye-catching policy is to put some of the cash towards deer management, including targeted culling.

Booming deer populations in The Broads are becoming a growing issue as the animals can cause damage to the environment through grazing.

People can submit their views as part of a consultation - which opened on 17 September and runs until 27 October - before Natural England submits its final plans to Eagle and her department.

Natural England hopes to roll out EDPs in other parts of England in the future.

The chief executive of Norfolk Wildlife Trust, Eliot Lyne, said his organisation needed more time to review the proposals.

But he said it was worried about wider changes to planning rules and how they affected natural habitats .

"We are concerned that it weakens existing protections for Norfolk's nationally and globally important wildlife sites such as chalk streams, wetlands and valley fens," he added.

Mark Dye, a chalk stream campaigner for the Gaywood River Revival group in west Norfolk, said: "Fundamentally, if you are polluting a chalk stream or a river and you're putting more and more pollution into that river, and not seeking to address the underlying causes of that, then it's only going to get worse."

Steve Turner, executive director of the Home Builders Federation, claimed pollution from farmers was a bigger issue than new homes and he criticised water companies for not investing in infrastructure to stop sewage entering rivers.
